question: A 29-year-old woman, obese, with no history of interest, who consulted for a bilateral, intense, pulsatile headache lasting one month, accompanied by horizontal diplopia and episodes of monocular amaurosis of seconds duration. The exploration is normal, except for the presence of bilateral papilledema. Which of these tests do you think will allow you to fully confirm your diagnosis ?:
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Bilateral, intense, pulsatile headache" -> "Horizontal diplopia" -> "Episodes of monocular amaurosis" -> "Bilateral papilledema" -> "Increased intracranial pressure" -> "Possible idiopathic intracranial hypertension" -> "Magnetic resonance of the skull" -> 85% CHAIN: "Bilateral papilledema" -> "Suspicion of increased intracranial pressure" -> "Lumbar puncture" -> 80% CHAIN: "Episodes of monocular amaurosis" -> "Possible optic nerve dysfunction" -> "Visual evoked potentials" -> 85%
enhanced_information: The patient's presentation of bilateral, intense, pulsatile headache, horizontal diplopia, episodes of monocular amaurosis, and bilateral papilledema suggests increased intracranial pressure, possibly idiopathic intracranial hypertension. The most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis is a lumbar puncture, given the suspicion of increased intracranial pressure associated with bilateral papilledema.
analysis: The presence of bilateral papilledema in a young obese woman with intense pulsatile headaches, horizontal diplopia, and transient monocular amaurosis suggests increased intracranial pressure. The most appropriate test to confirm the diagnosis in this case is a Lumbar puncture to measure the opening pressure and analyze the cerebrospinal fluid.
